tokyo-in-layers.story: Tokyo reads best as a set of distinct urban districts. The official visitor directory groups its recommendations by area, from central and eastern neighborhoods to western Tokyo, southern Tokyo, Tama, and the islands; choose one cluster before adding another.
tokyo-in-layers.visitPlan: Choose one area cluster as the day’s anchor, then use the official operator route planner to connect its stops. The clusters are an editorial way to keep a large city legible, not a verified timed itinerary.
tokyo-in-layers.access: Tokyo has extensive rail and subway coverage. The official visitor guide describes subway lines and additional railway operators; use the operator route tools for the chosen districts and travel date.

senso-ji-and-asakusa-lanes.story: Asakusa’s appeal comes from how its temple approach, neighborhood streets and Sumida waterfront sit within an easy walking area. GO TOKYO links Sensoji, Kaminarimon and Nakamise with nearby river views; the district lets a visitor move from a busy gate to the open river edge without changing neighborhoods.
senso-ji-and-asakusa-lanes.visitPlan: A source-listed walking sequence begins at Asakusa Station, then passes the Asakusa Culture Tourist Information Center, Kaminarimon, Nakamise Shopping Street and Sensoji. Kappabashi is a possible extension; treat the sequence as a walking outline, not a timed itinerary.
senso-ji-and-asakusa-lanes.access: Asakusa Station is served by the Tokyo Metro Ginza Line, Toei Asakusa Line and Tobu Skytree Line. GO TOKYO lists approximately 20 minutes from Tokyo Station and 35 minutes from Shinjuku Station, with transfers; confirm current service.

tokyo-skytree.story: TOKYO SKYTREE is more than a skyline stop: the approach is part of the visit. Its official transport guide points visitors to either Tokyo Skytree Station or Oshiage (Skytree-mae) Station, connecting the observation visit to the surrounding Sumida district.
tokyo-skytree.visitPlan: Check the official date-specific ticket inventory before choosing a time. If visiting both decks, confirm the ticket covers the Tembo Deck and Tembo Galleria; opening hours and prices can change by date.
tokyo-skytree.access: The official venue identifies Tokyo Skytree Station on the Tobu Skytree Line and Oshiage Station on the Hanzomon Line as convenient arrivals. The official site lists the address as 1-1-2 Oshiage, Sumida-ku, Tokyo.

rail.detail: Arrive at Tokyo Skytree Station or Oshiage (Skytree-mae) Station; use the official access page for specific approaches.

sado-island-s-wild-coast.story: Sado’s island story moves between exile history, gold mining, Kodo drumming, rice-growing landscapes and the Japanese crested ibis. Its scale matters: treat the port crossing as the start of a longer stay rather than assuming an island circuit fits a quick stop.
sado-island-s-wild-coast.visitPlan: Choose one side of Sado as a base and plan around the ferry port and current local transport. The national tourism guide notes that Sado can be visited in a day, but recommends an overnight stay; a short stay will leave large distances between experiences.
sado-island-s-wild-coast.access: Sado is reached by ferry. The Niigata–Ryotsu route has car ferries and jetfoils; the Naoetsu–Ogi route is seasonal and may not run in winter. Confirm the ferry operator timetable and fares for your date before booking connections.

kumano-kodo-the-old-paths.story: Kumano Kodo is a network of pilgrimage paths, not one single walk. The Nakahechi is the core route through the Kii mountains; its history, mountain setting and linked shrine paths reward a slower, section-by-section plan.
kumano-kodo-the-old-paths.visitPlan: Select a specific route section before planning accommodation or transit. The official bureau lists separate stages from Takijiri-oji toward Tsugizakura-oji and Kumano Hongu Taisha, plus shorter routes. The bureau describes the setting as mountainous and recommends preparation for multi-day walks.
kumano-kodo-the-old-paths.access: The Tanabe City Kumano Tourism Bureau says local buses reach isolated villages used as accommodation bases and publishes route maps, safety notes and route sections. Check the selected section and bus timetable before setting out.

mount-takao.story: Mount Takao pairs a compact mountain outing with a staffed visitor center at the summit. The center is not just a viewpoint stop: Tokyo’s nature-park authority describes exhibits and guides that can help visitors choose trails and understand the mountain’s nature and history.
mount-takao.visitPlan: Use the visitor center as a route decision point, not a promise that every trail is suitable. The authority lists the summit at 599 metres and describes a final walk from the cable-car or lift area; choose a trail after checking current conditions and your own ability.
mount-takao.access: The official visitor-center page gives its location as 2176 Takao-machi, Hachioji-shi, Tokyo. From Takaosanguchi Station, the page describes a five-minute walk to the cable-car/lift area and about 40 minutes on foot from the upper station to the center.

izu-peninsula-the-long-way-round.story: Izu makes more sense as a set of bases than as one hurried loop. The official national tourism guide separates eastern resort towns such as Atami and Ito from Shimoda in the south, the rugged capes, and the peninsula’s inland highlands; it advises allowing several days to explore.
izu-peninsula-the-long-way-round.visitPlan: Pick one base—such as Atami, Ito or Shimoda—and build a focused day around that area. The JNTO guide identifies the Shinkansen route from Tokyo to Atami, but this does not make the far-south or west-coast sights a same-day extension.
izu-peninsula-the-long-way-round.access: The JNTO guide lists Tokyo Station to Atami by Tokaido Shinkansen at about 50 minutes, with the Odoriko limited express and slower Tokaido Line as alternatives. Confirm the current timetable and continue from Atami according to the selected Izu area.

nikko-in-the-cedars.story: Nikko's sacred approach begins at Shinkyo Bridge, where the Daiya River marks the threshold to the mountain precinct. Follow the cedar-lined landscape through Rinnoji, Toshogu, Futarasan-jinja and Taiyuin: Buddhist halls, a vividly carved shogun's shrine, a mountain deity's sanctuary and the mausoleum of Tokugawa Iemitsu.
nikko-in-the-cedars.visitPlan: Take the World Heritage Sightseeing Bus from Tobu-Nikko Station to Shinkyo, then explore the five ordered stops on foot. Return from the Taiyuin/Futarasan-jinja bus stop. Total time and per-stop visit durations are omitted because no authoritative source for this exact sequence was found. Check operator hours and allow a flexible day.
nikko-in-the-cedars.access: From Tokyo, Tobu limited express trains connect Asakusa with Tobu-Nikko in about two hours; JNTO lists about 1 hour 40 minutes via Tohoku Shinkansen to Utsunomiya and JR Nikko Line. From Tobu-Nikko Station, the World Heritage bus reaches Shinkyo in about five minutes. Current timetables and fares vary.
